items.prompt: A service emits order events and different consumers need different reactions. Which EventBridge architecture expresses the routing boundary?
constraints: The producer should not know all consumers.
Consumers need separate target behavior.
Events are JSON with a stable contract.

options.text: Publish events to an EventBridge bus and create rules with event patterns that route matching events to independently configured targets.
Have the producer invoke every consumer directly because EventBridge rules cannot route one event to multiple targets.
Use a security group because EventBridge routes events by network port instead of event content.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle policies route JSON events to services by object age.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge rules match events and send them to configured targets, decoupling the producer from consumer-specific routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An event bus receives events, rules evaluate event patterns, and targets define the destination and invocation parameters. One event can match multiple rules.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team keeps producer schemas stable, assigns target ownership, and tests matching, nonmatching, and failed-target behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct producer fan-out couples services, security groups do not inspect event content, and lifecycle rules do not route EventBridge events.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Rule-based routing improves decoupling but can create overlapping matches and duplicate downstream invocations that consumers must handle.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EventBridge rules can route one event to multiple targets without producer changes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EventBridge matches event fields and is not routed by security-group ports.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 lifecycle manages objects and does not route EventBridge events.

items.prompt: A rule should match only successful payment events from the checkout service in production. Which pattern should be written?
constraints: The event includes source, detail-type, environment, and status.
Other services publish to the same bus.
False positives are costly.

options.text: Use an EventBridge event pattern that constrains the required source, detail-type, environment, and status fields, then test exact, missing, and extra-field cases.
Match only on event time because EventBridge treats timestamp equality as proof of source and business status.
Match every event on the bus and filter in the target because EventBridge patterns cannot inspect nested detail fields.
Use an IAM policy condition as the event pattern because IAM conditions are automatically evaluated against event detail fields.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge patterns match supported event fields and should constrain enough context to avoid routing unrelated events.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Patterns evaluate event envelope and detail fields using EventBridge matching operators. Pattern behavior should be tested against actual event shapes and missing fields.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates producer schema, deploys the rule, and monitors unexpected target invocations after event changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Time alone does not identify a business event, target-side filtering wastes delivery, and IAM conditions are not EventBridge event patterns.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Stricter patterns reduce false positives but can drop events when producers evolve the schema without coordinated changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Timestamp does not identify the source or successful payment status.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EventBridge patterns can inspect detail fields; broad matching increases downstream work and false positives.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM policy conditions authorize API actions and do not match event detail for a rule.

items.prompt: A central security account owns an EventBridge bus, and member accounts must send selected security events to it without reading or administering the bus. Which boundary is needed?
constraints: Member accounts are in one organization.
Only selected events cross the boundary.
The central account owns rules and targets.

options.text: Use an event-bus resource policy that permits the approved accounts or organization to PutEvents, and keep central bus rule, target, and administration permissions separate.
Grant member accounts events:* because cross-account event buses require full EventBridge administration in the sender account.
Use VPC peering because event-bus resource policies cannot authorize cross-account PutEvents.
Make the bus public so every member can publish without account or organization conditions.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge event-bus resource policies can authorize cross-account PutEvents while preserving centralized ownership of routing and targets.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The destination bus policy controls who can send events. Sender identity permissions and organization or account conditions can scope the path; sending does not grant bus administration.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security tests approved and unapproved accounts, constrains source events, and monitors failed PutEvents and central target delivery.
Details.errorCorrection: Full administration is unnecessary, VPC peering does not grant EventBridge API authorization, and public access weakens the boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central buses simplify aggregation but add policy, schema, and ownership dependencies across accounts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Member accounts need PutEvents, not unrestricted EventBridge administration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network connectivity does not replace the event-bus resource policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A public bus is not an acceptable substitute for organization- or account-scoped authorization.

items.prompt: A team wants to separate application-domain events from AWS service events and restrict who can publish to each domain. Which EventBridge resource should it create?
constraints: Domains have separate owners.
Event patterns and permissions differ.
The default bus should remain available for AWS events.

options.text: Create a custom event bus per appropriate domain or ownership boundary, publish application events there, and apply bus-specific policies and rules.
Put every event on the default bus because custom buses cannot receive application events or have their own rules.
Use one SQS queue as the event bus because queues provide EventBridge resource-policy isolation automatically.
Use an IAM group as a bus because group membership is the EventBridge routing boundary for domain events.

feedback.Reason: Custom event buses provide ownership and policy boundaries for application events separate from the default AWS event bus.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A custom bus receives events from supported producers and has its own rules, targets, and resource policy. The default bus is a separate event path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform maps domain ownership, grants PutEvents to producers, and keeps routing rules and target permissions with the consuming domain.
Details.errorCorrection: Custom buses can receive application events, SQS is a queue rather than a bus, and IAM groups do not define event routing.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple buses improve isolation but increase cross-bus routing and operational inventory.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Custom buses are intended for application events and can have their own rules and policies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: SQS buffers messages and does not provide an EventBridge bus and rule model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM groups organize identity permissions and do not represent event buses.

items.prompt: A consumer is added after important domain events were published, and the team needs to replay retained events within an approved time window. Which EventBridge capability should be configured?
constraints: Only selected events should be retained.
Retention has a defined duration.
Replay must not blindly duplicate side effects.

options.text: Configure an EventBridge archive with an event pattern and retention period, then plan controlled replay and idempotent target processing.
Use CloudTrail event history because it automatically archives every custom event and replays it to any EventBridge target.
Use an SQS visibility timeout because it stores events after they have been acknowledged by all targets.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle can replay expired EventBridge events into new targets.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge archives retain matching events and support replay, but replay is a new delivery that requires side-effect safety.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An archive filters and retains events for a configured period; a replay sends matching historical events to a target event bus and does not undo prior processing.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner filters the archive, validates the new consumer in a staging path, replays by time range, and monitors duplicates and failures.
Details.errorCorrection: CloudTrail is not a generic custom-event replay store, visibility timeout does not retain acknowledged events, and S3 lifecycle cannot replay EventBridge events.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Archives improve recoverability and late-consumer onboarding but add storage cost and replay duplication risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudTrail is not the archive and replay mechanism for custom EventBridge events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Visibility timeout controls queue redelivery and does not archive bus events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 lifecycle rules do not replay EventBridge events.

items.prompt: A repaired consumer should receive only events from yesterday between 10:00 and 11:00, and live events must continue during the replay. What should the runbook specify?
constraints: The archive contains more than the desired range.
Live processing continues.
The consumer is idempotent or replay-isolated.

options.text: Start an EventBridge replay with the exact archive and time range, choose the target bus or routing path deliberately, and monitor replayed versus live event effects.
Replay the entire archive because EventBridge cannot select a time range or target event bus for replay.
Stop all event producers permanently because replay and live delivery cannot coexist in EventBridge.
Use an SQS queue purge because purging a queue causes EventBridge to regenerate the requested historical events.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge replay should be scoped to the archive and time interval that represents the recovery need and coordinated with live delivery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replay selects events from an archive within a time range and sends them to a chosen event bus. Replayed events can match rules and invoke targets again.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operations tests the consumer with a narrow range, observes duplicate and ordering behavior, and pauses or isolates downstream side effects when necessary.
Details.errorCorrection: Full-archive replay increases impact, live delivery can coexist with replay, and queue purge does not recreate EventBridge history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Scoped replay reduces blast radius but still requires consumer idempotency and target-rate controls.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EventBridge replay can be scoped and should not replay unrelated history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Replay and live delivery can coexist; stopping producers is not the normal mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SQS purge deletes queue messages and cannot regenerate EventBridge archive events.

items.prompt: A target service is temporarily unavailable and EventBridge should retry delivery for a bounded period before declaring failure. Which behavior should be configured?
constraints: The target can recover.
Retry should not continue forever.
Failed events need an observable path.

options.text: Configure the EventBridge target retry policy with maximum event age and retry attempts, then add a DLQ or failure notification and make the target idempotent.
Use unlimited retries because EventBridge guarantees that repeated target invocation has no side effects.
Disable retries because one failed target invocation permanently removes the event from the bus.
Use a security group timeout because EventBridge retry policy is determined by network connection lifetime.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge target retry policies bound retry age and attempts; exhausted failures need a DLQ or operational alert.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EventBridge retries failed target delivery according to the target policy. A retry is another invocation, so target side effects must be idempotent or deduplicated.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models target recovery time, configures maximum age and attempts, and inspects failed events instead of silently losing them.
Details.errorCorrection: Unlimited retries can overload a recovering target, disabling retries loses recoverable events, and network timeouts do not configure EventBridge retries.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Longer retry windows improve delivery resilience but delay failure visibility and can increase duplicate target invocations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Repeated delivery can duplicate side effects and should be bounded.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EventBridge can retry failed delivery; disabling it discards a recovery opportunity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retry policy is an EventBridge target setting and not a security-group timeout.

items.prompt: A critical EventBridge target can fail after all configured retries, and operations must inspect the original event and error context. Which target configuration is appropriate?
constraints: The event must not disappear silently.
The target is independently owned.
Replay requires an explicit operator decision.

options.text: Configure a target DLQ with the required SQS permissions, alert on its depth and age, and replay or redrive only after the target failure is understood.
Rely on the event bus archive only because an archive automatically receives every target delivery failure regardless of configuration.
Delete the failed event because EventBridge target failures are not actionable after retry exhaustion.
Use a Route 53 health check as the DLQ because health checks store failed event payloads for later delivery.

feedback.Reason: A target DLQ preserves events that could not be delivered to that target after retry exhaustion, with its own queue and access policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EventBridge sends failed target events to a configured SQS DLQ when supported. An archive is a separate event-retention path and does not automatically capture every target failure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner grants EventBridge SendMessage, monitors DLQ age, and replays only after fixing the target and checking idempotency.
Details.errorCorrection: Archives and target DLQs have different semantics, deleting loses the event, and Route 53 health checks do not store payloads.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A DLQ adds durable failure handling but needs retention, cost, security, and replay ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An archive does not automatically capture every target delivery failure; the target DLQ must be configured.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retry exhaustion should produce observable failure evidence rather than silent deletion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks report endpoint state and do not store EventBridge event payloads.

items.prompt: A target needs only orderId and customerTier, while the source event contains internal fields that must not be forwarded. Which rule feature should be used?
constraints: The target contract is smaller.
Internal fields must be excluded.
The source event remains unchanged for other consumers.

options.text: Use an EventBridge input transformer or target input mapping to select and reshape approved fields for that target, then test missing-field behavior.
Mutate the original event before publishing because all EventBridge targets must receive the same reduced payload.
Use an SQS visibility timeout because it removes unwanted JSON fields before the target receives a message.
Use KMS encryption because encrypted events automatically hide selected fields from a target without transformation.

feedback.Reason: Input transformers shape a target’s payload without changing the canonical event delivered to other rules and consumers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EventBridge can extract values from the matched event and construct a target input. The mapping must account for absent paths and target schema requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner maps only approved fields, tests missing and null values, and avoids leaking source-only metadata to external targets.
Details.errorCorrection: Mutating the source harms other consumers, visibility timeout is queue redelivery control, and encryption does not select JSON fields.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Per-target transformation supports decoupled contracts but adds mapping maintenance and possible data-loss ambiguity if fields are absent.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Other consumers may need the canonical event, so mutation at publish time couples all targets to one reduced shape.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Visibility timeout does not transform JSON payloads.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encryption protects data and does not construct a target-specific payload.

items.prompt: A Step Functions target needs the nested workflow ARN and tenant ID from an event, but no other event data. What should be configured?
constraints: The fields are at known JSON paths.
The target input must be minimal.
The source event is shared by other targets.

options.text: Use an EventBridge input path or transformer to select the nested values and construct the target input, then validate the resulting JSON against the Step Functions contract.
Pass the entire event because EventBridge cannot select nested fields for a target input.
Use a security group because nested JSON paths are represented by protocol ports.
Use an IAM permission boundary because it removes fields from EventBridge target requests.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge target input mapping can select values from the event and keep each target contract explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Input paths and transformers extract fields from the matched event; the mapping must be tested for missing or incorrectly typed values.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps the shared event canonical, passes only target-approved data, and treats transformation failures as observable integration errors.
Details.errorCorrection: Passing all fields violates the minimal contract, security groups do not parse JSON, and boundaries do not remove fields.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Target-specific mapping reduces coupling and exposure but adds schema tests and maintenance when event paths evolve.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EventBridge supports target input selection and passing the entire event creates unnecessary coupling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network ports do not represent nested JSON paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM boundaries constrain permissions and do not transform event payloads.

items.prompt: Multiple teams publish domain events and need a discoverable contract for event structure and versions. Which EventBridge capability should be evaluated?
constraints: Events have producers and consumers.
Schema changes require review.
Developers need generated or discoverable definitions.

options.text: Use EventBridge Schemas or a schema registry for approved event definitions and version discovery, while retaining compatibility and ownership review in the producer contract.
Use CloudWatch metrics because a metric name and value fully define the event schema for every consumer.
Use an SQS DLQ as the schema registry because failed messages automatically become the canonical event definition.
Use a security group because event schemas are network contracts represented by allowed ports.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge Schemas supports discovery and management of event definitions, but teams still govern compatibility and semantic ownership.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A schema registry stores or discovers event schemas and versions. It does not automatically make producers compatible or authorize consumers.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform registers events, reviews changes, and tests consumers against compatible versions before publishing a breaking change.
Details.errorCorrection: Metrics do not define full event contracts, DLQs contain failures rather than canonical schemas, and ports are not event definitions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Schema discovery reduces integration ambiguity but introduces versioning and governance overhead.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Metrics do not capture the full structure, semantics, and versioning of an event.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A DLQ stores failed messages and is not a schema registry.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network ports do not describe event payload contracts.

items.prompt: A team has unknown event producers and wants to discover schemas from events before defining a shared contract. Which feature should be used carefully?
constraints: The source events may contain sensitive fields.
Discovery is not approval.
Producers may evolve independently.

options.text: Use EventBridge schema discovery in a controlled event environment, review generated schemas for accuracy and sensitive data, and publish approved versions through governance.
Treat every generated schema as authoritative because discovery guarantees semantic correctness and backward compatibility.
Disable access controls during discovery so the registry can inspect every account and event source automatically.
Use a public S3 bucket for discovered schemas because schemas are never sensitive and need no owner.

feedback.Reason: Schema discovery can accelerate understanding of event shape but does not replace review, privacy, or compatibility governance.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Discovery observes events and generates schema suggestions. The result can reflect examples rather than all valid cases and may expose fields that need classification.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner limits discovery scope, reviews data, assigns schema ownership, and validates consumers before making a version canonical.
Details.errorCorrection: Generated schemas are not semantic guarantees, disabling access controls is unsafe, and public schema storage can expose sensitive structure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Discovery reduces initial authoring work but can create false confidence or leak data if examples and ownership are unmanaged.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Discovery reflects observed examples and cannot guarantee semantics or compatibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Discovery still requires least-privilege access and controlled event scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Schemas can contain sensitive fields and need ownership and access controls.

items.prompt: A team needs to filter and enrich messages from a supported queue before sending them to a target, with less custom polling code. Which EventBridge capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The source and target are supported.
Filtering and transformation are required.
The message flow should remain observable.

options.text: Evaluate EventBridge Pipes for the supported source, filtering, enrichment, and target path, then configure permissions, batching, retries, and failure handling explicitly.
Use a security group because Pipes automatically reads and transforms messages based on network membership.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle policies provide generic queue-to-target enrichment.
Use direct producer-to-target calls because Pipes cannot read from queues or apply filters.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge Pipes provides a managed point-to-point source-filter-enrichment-target path for supported integrations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Pipes connect a source to a target with optional filtering and enrichment. They still require source and target permissions, batching, retries, and monitoring.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner verifies support and semantics, configures least privilege, and tests partial failure and poison-message behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups do not transform messages, lifecycle rules do not enrich queues, and direct calls reintroduce producer-target coupling.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pipes reduce custom glue code but add a managed integration whose limits and failure behavior must be understood.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Pipes are service integrations and not network membership rules.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 lifecycle does not connect queues to targets or enrich messages.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Pipes are specifically intended to reduce custom point-to-point polling and transformation code for supported paths.

items.prompt: A consumer assumes that two events from different producers will always arrive at a target in publish order. What correction is needed?
constraints: The target is invoked asynchronously.
Events may be retried.
Business order is important for one entity.

options.text: Do not rely on general EventBridge ordering; include an entity sequence or version in the event, and use a FIFO or ordered workflow design when strict ordering is required.
Assume EventBridge preserves global ordering because one event bus has one logical stream for all producers.
Use a security group because packet order guarantees EventBridge target order across retries.
Increase target retry attempts because more retries convert asynchronous delivery into ordered delivery.

feedback.Reason: General EventBridge routing and retries should not be treated as a global ordering guarantee.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Events can be delivered asynchronously, matched by multiple rules, and retried. Ordering requirements need an explicit sequence, consumer logic, or a service with the required FIFO semantics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The producer adds entity version or sequence, and the consumer rejects stale events or uses an ordered queue where required.
Details.errorCorrection: A single bus does not guarantee global event order, network packet order is not target order, and retries can increase reordering.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Explicit ordering logic adds state and complexity but avoids silently applying stale events.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EventBridge is not a general global ordered log for all producers and targets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network packet order does not define asynchronous target delivery order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: More retries can increase duplicate and out-of-order deliveries rather than guarantee order.

items.prompt: A rule target creates an external ticket and may receive the same EventBridge event more than once after a timeout. Which application contract is required?
constraints: Target invocation is asynchronous.
The side effect is not naturally idempotent.
Events contain a stable ID.

options.text: Use the EventBridge event ID or a business idempotency key to make ticket creation conditional, and delete or acknowledge downstream work only after durable success.
Assume EventBridge invokes each target exactly once because a rule matches an event only once.
Use a security group to prevent a repeated target request from reaching the ticket service.
Disable target retries because duplicate side effects are impossible after a timeout.

feedback.Reason: Asynchronous event delivery and retries require idempotent target side effects.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A target may be invoked again after a transient failure or ambiguous timeout. The event ID or business key can support deduplication in durable state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service writes a unique ticket key transactionally, treats repeated events as no-ops, and monitors retry and DLQ outcomes.
Details.errorCorrection: A rule match does not guarantee exactly-once side effects, security groups do not deduplicate events, and disabling retries loses recoverable delivery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Idempotency adds state and cleanup but is safer than relying on delivery assumptions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EventBridge delivery and target side effects are not an exactly-once transaction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network controls do not detect repeated business event IDs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling retries discards a recovery path and does not solve already ambiguous side effects.

items.prompt: A cleanup operation should invoke a target every hour without deploying a server or adding a polling loop. Which EventBridge feature is appropriate?
constraints: The schedule is time-based.
The target is an AWS service or function.
The operation must remain observable and authorized.

options.text: Use an EventBridge scheduled rule or supported scheduler capability with a target, least-privilege invocation role, and retry or failure handling.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle invokes arbitrary Lambda functions at an exact hourly schedule for any service.
Use a security group because security-group refresh intervals schedule application operations.
Use a CloudWatch dashboard because dashboards execute the target whenever the page is viewed.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge scheduled rules can invoke supported targets on a time-based expression without a polling server.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A schedule rule emits an event on its configured schedule and invokes a target through an IAM role or service permission as required.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests time zone and retry behavior, scopes the target role, and alerts on failed invocations.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 lifecycle is an object lifecycle service, security groups do not schedule jobs, and dashboards are visualization resources.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed scheduling removes servers but requires attention to duplicate invocations, time semantics, and target idempotency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 lifecycle does not provide a general hourly scheduler for arbitrary service operations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups do not schedule application work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A dashboard displays metrics and does not execute targets on view.

items.prompt: A producer adds a field to an event and a consumer has old code that ignores unknown fields, but another consumer requires a new field. What is the safest evolution?
constraints: Consumers are deployed independently.
The old contract must keep working.
The new consumer has a clear version need.

options.text: Add compatible fields or introduce an explicit event version and route consumers deliberately, validating schema compatibility before publishing a breaking change.
Replace the event shape immediately because EventBridge rules automatically translate all old consumers to the new schema.
Hide the version in a security group because event contracts are network metadata rather than payload contracts.
Delete the old rule before deploying the producer because one event type should have only one consumer version.

feedback.Reason: Event contracts are shared boundaries and must evolve compatibly or through explicit versions when producers and consumers deploy independently.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EventBridge routes fields but does not automatically translate semantic schema changes for targets. Rules, schemas, and consumers must agree on version behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform publishes a compatible event or versioned detail-type, tests both consumers, and retires old routes only after usage evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Rules do not translate schemas, security groups do not carry event versions, and deleting the old rule before migration can drop events.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Versioned events and routes add compatibility work but prevent independent deployment from becoming a breaking release.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EventBridge matching does not translate arbitrary old consumer contracts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Event versions belong in the event contract, not network metadata.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retiring a rule before consumer migration can drop or misroute events.

items.prompt: A platform needs content-based routing, event archive and replay, cross-account buses, and multiple service targets. Which service boundary is the strongest starting point?
constraints: The producer publishes events rather than direct notifications.
Rules must inspect event fields.
Replay and routing ownership matter.

options.text: Evaluate EventBridge for event buses, content-based rules, archive and replay, and cross-account routing; use SNS when simple topic fan-out and notification semantics are the primary need.
Use SQS alone because queues provide content-based event-bus rules, archives, and cross-account routing without consumers.
Use API Gateway because API routes automatically archive and replay asynchronous domain events.
Use CloudWatch metrics because metrics can route arbitrary JSON events to multiple targets and preserve them for replay.

feedback.Reason: EventBridge is designed for event buses, pattern rules, cross-account event routing, and archive or replay workflows; SNS remains a strong simple fan-out choice.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EventBridge rules and buses provide content-aware routing and event lifecycle features. The selection should reflect whether the system needs event-bus semantics or straightforward topic notification.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect maps producer ownership, target delivery, replay, schema, and failure needs before choosing or combining services.
Details.errorCorrection: SQS queues do not provide EventBridge bus rules, API Gateway is an API boundary, and metrics are not JSON event stores.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: EventBridge adds richer routing and lifecycle controls, while SNS may be simpler and lower overhead for pure pub/sub fan-out.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SQS provides buffering and consumer semantics but not EventBridge content-based bus routing and archive features.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: API Gateway exposes APIs and does not automatically archive or replay domain events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Metrics are aggregates and cannot route or replay arbitrary event payloads.
